ai.blurb: Flies bomber aircraft and commands the crew, planning and carrying out long-range strike and training missions.

Expect exams, case reviews and a lot of conversation with industrial hygienists, bioenvironmental engineers, public health and safety staff about noise, chemicals, water supply and immunisations. Much of the job is advisory: deciding whether someone is fit for a particular task, and whether that task is safe for anyone.
ai.funFact: Occupational medicine is one of the few specialties where the patient is partly the workplace itself — the discipline grew out of industrial-era findings that certain trades reliably made their workers ill.

Prevention interests you more than heroics
You like working across technical teams

The pace swings between careful monitoring and sudden emergencies, and shifts include nights and weekends because critical patients don't keep office hours.

You manage most cases independently, and collaborate with OB/GYNs or family practice physicians when something more complicated comes up. You also look after the newborn in the hours and days after delivery until mother and baby go home.
ai.funFact: Nurse midwives are advanced practice registered nurses, and the credential here is civilian: certification by the American Midwifery Certification Board is required before you can hold the AFSC.

calm during long, unpredictable shifts

want to care for military families

ai.funFact: Nurse anaesthesia is one of the oldest advanced nursing roles in the US, with nurses administering anaesthetics on battlefields since the Civil War era.

You also act as a teacher and consultant to other staff, which means explaining your reasoning as much as making decisions.

The pace is clinic-steady rather than emergency-driven, with records, treatment plans and coordination with general dentists and oral surgeons filling the gaps. You also teach: instructing dental officers and technicians in orthodontic procedures is part of the job.

You run the pathology service, so there's administration and teaching alongside the microscope work, plus consultations with oral surgeons, hospital boards and committees. The pace is steady and considered rather than frantic — the pressure comes from getting the answer right.
ai.funFact: Oral and maxillofacial pathology is one of the smallest recognised dental specialties, and reaching it means a dental degree plus a full residency before you ever wear the uniform.

The state-of-the-art analysis provided by these experts not only helps prevent and treat disease, but is essential to detecting agents that indicate biological warfare.
duties: Test and analyze specimens using laboratory techniques
Complete processing of blood for transfusion
Perform chemical analysis and blood bank duties
Keep lab conditions safe and organized
Maintain records of all laboratory work performed
Assist biological warfare officer in developing procedures to detect bacteriological agents

Completion of 7.5 weeks of Basic Military Training
Must be at least 17, but has not reached age 42 on the date of enlistment
You must be 17–42 years of age, a U.S. citizen and obtain a qualifying ASVAB score.

Status Upon Completion: Enlisted Airman with credits earned towards Medical Laboratory Technology

ai.blurb: Runs lab tests on blood and other specimens so doctors can diagnose and treat patients correctly.
ai.dayToDay: You work indoors in a hospital or clinic laboratory, mostly at benches and analysers, processing specimens that arrive from doctors, nurses and the emergency room. Expect careful, repetitive, detail-heavy work: running chemistry panels, cross-matching blood for transfusion, logging every result, and keeping the lab clean and orderly. Labs run around the clock, so shift work is normal, and you'll rarely meet the patients whose samples you handle.
ai.funFact: Air Force lab techs aren't only looking for disease — the career field also supports detecting bacteriological agents, assisting the biological warfare officer with identification procedures.
goodFitIf: like precise, methodical work
can concentrate for long stretches
are interested in medicine, not bedside care
have normal colour vision

ai.blurb: Prepares tissue samples in a hospital lab so pathologists can diagnose disease, and assists at autopsies.
ai.dayToDay: You work indoors in a hospital laboratory,处理 surgical specimens: receiving them, cutting and mounting thin sections, staining slides and logging everything so nothing is mixed up. Much of the day is careful bench work with microtomes, chemicals and record-keeping, alongside pathologists and other lab technicians. You may also assist during autopsies as a technical assistant, and help keep the lab's instruments and accreditation standards in order.
ai.funFact: Normal colour vision is a hard requirement — histology diagnosis depends on stains like haematoxylin and eosin, which turn tissue blue and pink under the microscope.

Biology and chemistry interested you at school

You like careful record-keeping

You lead teams of enlisted cyber Airmen who keep systems running and watch for intrusions, and you translate what commanders need into technical designs. Networks don't observe office hours, so shift work and late-night callouts come with the job.
ai.funFact: The Air Force treats cyberspace as a warfighting domain alongside air and space, which is why network officers sit in the same operational conversations as pilots.

title: Cyberspace Effects Operations Officer

A Cyber Warfare Operations Officer commands a crew and is in charge of cyberspace weapons systems. Combat communications, missile guidance systems, the nation’s power grid, rocket launches…all depend on cybersecurity in the battle space above our planet. Maintaining vigilance across all cyber channels and working with and advising commanders, this officer assesses intelligence information, plans and executes missions, and ensures his or her team and all equipment is mission-ready at all times.

You review intelligence and mission tasking, brief and debrief your crew, oversee mission planning, and advise commanders on what's possible in the cyber domain. ai.blurb: Keeps the Air Force's ground fleet running — everything from forklifts and dump trucks to cranes and snow blowers.
ai.dayToDay: You work in a base vehicle maintenance shop alongside other mechanics, diagnosing faults, pulling electrical components, and doing scheduled inspections on an odd assortment of heavy and specialist vehicles. The pace follows the base: routine servicing most days, long hours when something critical breaks or the weather turns and the snow equipment is suddenly the most important thing on the airfield. Expect grease, hazardous waste paperwork, and a driver's licence you'll actually use.
ai.funFact: Tech school for this job is at Port Hueneme in California — a Navy base, where the Air Force sends its vehicle mechanics for about 79 days of training.

you'd rather fix than file

ai.dayToDay: Training takes up a vast amount of the job: diving, parachuting, air traffic control certification and combat controller qualification, all of which must be kept current. On operations you plan and command small teams working alongside Army and Navy special operations units, often on austere strips far from any established base. Between deployments you're organising, training and equipping your team, and doing the staff work that goes with being an officer.
ai.funFact: Combat controllers, the enlisted specialty a Special Tactics Officer leads, carry the motto "First There" — their job is to arrive ahead of everyone else and turn a patch of dirt into a usable airfield.
goodFitIf: You lead from the front, not a desk
Water and heights don't bother you
You can hold a security clearance
You like detail under physical strain

title: Tactical Air Control Party (TACP) Officer - Requirements and Benefits
tagline: IN CHARGE OF BRINGING THE THUNDER
overview: There are few things that can change the course of battle like a properly executed air strike. As members of Air Force Special Warfare, Tactical Air Control Party (TACP) officers imbed with Army and Marine units on the frontline with the incredible responsibility of calling in an air strike on the right target at just the right time. These highly trained experts go through intense physical, mental and technical training in order to withstand the demanding conditions of battle and provide their team with the firepower they need for continued success on the battlefield.
duties: Engage enemy forces utilizing advanced technologies and weapon systems
Control and execute operational air and space power
Train in all major climatic conditions: arctic, desert, tropical, ocean and temperate
Operate and maintain cutting-edge technology, including communications, computers, digital networks, targeting and surveillance equipment and various special-purpose tactical vehicles
Target and control surface-to-surface and air-to-surface fires
Plan and execute fire missions to accomplish mission objectives
Engage enemy forces with individual weapons
Administer combat lifesaving assistance
requirements: Knowledge of maps and charts, command and control principles and procedures, survival techniques, field leadership and evasion
Completion of specialty training courses (JTAC)
Physical qualification to support parachute duty
Maintain physical fitness and combat-ready status

Completion of Officer Training School (OTS), Air Force Academy (AFA) or Air Force Reserve Officer Training Corp (AFROTC)

ai.blurb: Air Force officer who embeds with Army and Marine ground units and directs aircraft onto enemy targets.
ai.dayToDay: You lead a small team attached to a ground unit, often living and moving with soldiers or Marines rather than on an air base. Days swing between planning fire missions, maintaining radios, targeting gear and tactical vehicles, and long stretches of physical training; in the field you're carrying a weapon and a rucksack like everyone else. Training covers arctic, desert, tropical, ocean and temperate conditions, and you'll qualify for parachute duty and combat lifesaving.
ai.funFact: TACP personnel qualify as Joint Terminal Attack Controllers (JTACs) — the certification that legally authorises someone on the ground to clear an aircraft to drop ordnance.
goodFitIf: you want to lead from the front
you're comfortable being the only airman around
you handle sustained physical hardship well
you can stay calm making high-stakes calls

title: Combat Rescue Officer
overview: When servicemen are injured and rendered immobile on the front lines, their life depends on a swift, effective evacuation. Responsible for organizing and strategizing recovery operations, Combat Rescue Officers provide the insights and skill essential for rescue missions to succeed. These highly capable and courageous Airmen not only train, equip and develop necessary survival skills in rescue personnel, but will often deploy into direct combat as a member of the rescue team themselves.
duties: Provide command and control of full spectrum personnel recovery operations

Assess readiness through training exercises, inspections and evaluation results
Strategize and conduct rescue and recovery operations
Manage rescue programs and training
Direct short- and long-term survival and evasion assistance

ai.blurb: Plans and leads combat rescue missions to recover injured or isolated personnel, often going in with the team.
ai.dayToDay: Between deployments, most of the work is planning, training and assessing readiness — exercises, inspections, evaluations, and keeping rescue teams and SERE programs sharp. You lead Pararescuemen and survival specialists, which means you're expected to meet the same brutal physical standards they do: diving, static-line and free-fall jumping, underwater egress, SERE. On operations you're running command and control of a recovery, and sometimes you're on the aircraft and on the ground doing it yourself.
ai.funFact: The Air Force rescue community's motto is "These Things We Do, That Others May Live" — and Combat Rescue Officer is one of the few officer paths where you attend the same gruelling pipeline as the enlisted operators you'll lead.
goodFitIf: thrive under sustained physical punishment
want to lead from the front
are comfortable in water and air
can stay calm planning under pressure

title: SERE Specialist
overview: The strength of SERE specialists lies in their ability to prepare others for the critical Personal Recovery mission. They empower others with skills for survival, evasion, resistance, and escape in adverse conditions. They integrate with other Airmen, military peers, government entities, and foreign allies, in effort to bolster recovery initiatives that guarantee every participant is well-prepared to "return with honor".
duties: Prepare aircrew and high-risk-of-isolation personnel to return from any type of survival situation.
Train and operate in remote and austere environments, day or night.
Provide direct support to Personnel Recovery (PR) programs through preparation, planning, execution, and adaptation.
Conduct developmental and operational testing of SERE and Aircrew equipment.
Perform static line, military free fall, and emergency parachuting techniques in support of various operations and exercises.

ai.blurb: Teaches aircrew and other high-risk personnel how to survive, evade capture, resist interrogation and escape — then get home with honour.
ai.dayToDay: You spend a lot of time outdoors teaching: in mountains, desert, jungle, water and cold-weather sites, by day and night, often for days at a time with students who have never slept rough. Between courses you plan training, support personnel recovery programmes, and test survival and aircrew equipment. You also parachute — static line, military free fall and emergency techniques — in support of exercises and operations, and work alongside other services, agencies and allied forces.
ai.funFact: "Return with Honor" is the field's motto, and SERE instruction grew directly out of the experiences of American prisoners of war — the resistance training exists because former POWs told the military what they wished they had known.
goodFitIf: You teach well under pressure
You're comfortable living rough
You stay calm when others panic
You want a physically demanding instructor role

title: Explosive Ordnance Disposal Technician
overview: Mitigating the hazards of explosive materials and other weapons takes immense courage, precision, and skill. Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) members undertake some of the Air Force's most dangerous missions in diverse and unforgiving locales worldwide. These brave Airmen work solo or in teams and employ special tools and vehicles to safely locate, identify, recover, disarm, and dispose of dangerous weapons that threaten people, property, and natural environments.
duties: Maintain equipment, technical data and vehicles
Protect the president, vice president and other dignitaries
Analyze unknown munitions and explosives for intelligence agencies
Conduct nuclear weapon response
Detect, identify, recover, disarm and dispose of unsafe explosives and ordnance

ai.blurb: Finds, identifies and safely disposes of bombs, missiles and improvised explosive devices, often in hostile places.
ai.dayToDay: A lot of it is methodical: maintaining robots, vehicles, bomb suits and technical manuals, rehearsing procedures, and studying munitions from around the world. When a call comes, you work alone or in a small team to locate a device, work out what it is, and render it safe or blow it in place. Assignments range from deployed airfields to escorting the president's protective detail, and from nuclear weapon response to writing up findings for intelligence agencies.
ai.funFact: EOD technicians analyse recovered enemy munitions for intelligence agencies, so the job doubles as a form of technical detective work.
goodFitIf: You stay calm under real pressure
Methodical patience appeals to you
You want a Top Secret clearance role
Physical standards don't put you off
